digest.top_line: BEACON-HCC: 96.6% expert concordance vs 72.4% for BCLC 2025, and the new North American framework moves SBRT and TARE out of the salvage column.
digest.tldr: Hepatobiliary carried the day, and it was a staging story rather than a trial readout. BEACON's Delphi framework elevates SBRT and TARE as primary options in Classes 1A, 2 and 3A, and leaves the door open for local therapy in macrovascular invasion (Class 1D/3B) where BCLC calls it advanced. Note the evidence base: Class 3B rests on RTOG1112's OS trend only (p=0.06).

sites.intro: A 20-expert North American allocation framework that reclassifies where SBRT and TARE belong, built on 29 scored cases rather than patient outcomes.

details: 📊 Pilot concordance: 28 of 29 cases (96.6%) with BEACON vs 72.4% with BCLC 2025
📊 Class 3B leans on NRG/RTOG1112: SBRT vs sorafenib, Vp3/4 in 63%, OS trend only (p=0.06)
📊 Class 1D leans on DOSISPHERE: personalized dosimetry ORR 71 vs 36%, OS 26.6 vs 10.7 mo

subdetails: Recorded dissent: TARE should be preferred rather than useful; one respondent said SBRT

details: 💊 No adjuvant therapy after complete response to surgical or locoregional treatment
⚠️ Class 4A (>50% burden): TACE, TARE and EBRT not routinely indicated outside palliation
⚠️ 96.6% rests on 29 cases scored by experts, not on patient outcomes

verdict.rationale: Delphi consensus, not new trial data; BEACON's 96.6% concordance is circular (framework and raters share one practice community). The 72.4% BCLC gap is the defensible signal.

studies.significance: SBRT and TARE are elevated into Classes 1A, 2 and 3A, and TACE is named not preferred for Class 1B given lower ORR/CR and shorter TTP than radiation-based approaches. That is the tumor-board argument for offering SBRT in early unifocal disease. Dissent ran toward listing TARE, and for one respondent SBRT, as preferred rather than useful.
studies.monday_clinic: In a Child-Pugh A patient with unifocal HCC >3 to 8 cm who is not a surgical candidate (Class 1B), this supports SBRT or TARE over TACE as destination therapy; it does not extend to >50% tumor burden (Class 4A), where EBRT and TARE are not routinely indicated outside palliation.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Modified Delphi across **20 North American experts** in hepatology, medical oncology, surgery, radiology and radiation oncology, with iterative discussion and two voting rounds. Validated in a pilot of **29 real-world cases** scored by external multidisciplinary experts.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: EBRT/SBRT and TARE are **elevated** as locoregional options in Classes 1A, 2 and 3A, and named as potential therapy for Vp1-2 invasion in Class 1D. For Class 1B, TACE is **not preferred** versus radiation-based approaches given lower ORR/CR and shorter TTP. In **Class 4A** (>50% burden) they are not routinely indicated outside palliation.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: The single discordant case carried vascular invasion extending into the right atrium, where external experts chose **combined systemic plus locoregional therapy**, allowable in the framework but outside its standard recommendation. Combined systemic and local therapy was the preferred strategy in **7 of the 29 cases**.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Against **BCLC 2025** the same cases reached only **72.4% concordance**. Table 4 locates the divergence: BEACON splits BCLC's advanced stage C across Classes 1D, 3B and 4B, and elevates SBRT and TARE in classes where the stages otherwise align.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents multidisciplinary HCC treatment allocation in North American practice, Class 1A through 4B, across liver-function strata. Does not represent European or Asian practice patterns, nor patients with **ECOG PS ≥2** or **Child-Pugh ≥B9** ineligible for transplant, for whom symptom-directed care is the stated default.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The elevation of SBRT and TARE rests on cohort studies and small RCTs; the document itself states there are **few high-quality data demonstrating superiority of one locoregional therapy over another**, and no RCT compares personalized-dosimetry TARE against ICI systemic therapy in Class 1D. **Two respondents abstained on Class 3B in both rounds**, the class where the RT-versus-systemic question is sharpest.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: SBRT and TARE are elevated into Classes 1A, 2 and 3A, and TACE is named not preferred for Class 1B given lower ORR/CR and shorter TTP than radiation-based approaches. That is the tumor-board argument for offering SBRT in early unifocal disease. Class 3B still rests on RTOG1112's p=0.06 trend.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: Adjuvant systemic therapy after complete response stays off the table, and ICI plus TACE remains case-by-case rather than routine. The live systemic question is upstream: propensity-matched data suggest systemic therapy better preserves liver function and yields better OS than TACE for unifocal HCC >7 cm and beyond up-to-seven, now in an RCT.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: CSPH, not tumor diameter, is the resection-versus-transplant gate: both give 5-year survival >70%, but recurrence exceeds 50% at 5 years after resection versus 10-15% after LT. Class 3B becomes newly surgical: an RCT reported resection after neoadjuvant radiation outperformed up-front resection in that population.

papers.title: BEACON-HCC: Best evidence and north american consensus on treatment allocation for hepatocellular carcinoma
authors: on behalf of HCC-Live Steering Committee
papers.abstract: Background : Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains a major cause of cancer-related mortality. Optimal treatment decisions are challenging, and existing treatment allocation frameworks may not fully reflect the evolving therapeutic landscape or contemporary clinical practices in North America. Methods : Using a modified Delphi process, a multidisciplinary panel of 20 North American experts in hepatology, medical oncology, surgery, radiology, and radiation oncology developed a consensus-based treatment framework for HCC, termed the BEACON-HCC system. The framework was informed by current evidence and expert opinion through iterative discussion and voting. In a pilot study using 29 real-world patient cases, we assessed concordance between external expert recommendations and BEACON-HCC recommendations and Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer (BCLC) 2025 treatment recommendations. Results : The BEACON-HCC treatment allocation framework diverges from prior frameworks by incorporating nuanced clinical features such as degree of intrahepatic tumor burden and vascular invasion, and adverse tumor prognostic markers, to align treatment allocation with tumor biology and therapeutic potential. Key innovations include the incorporation of emerging modalities such as external beam radiation therapy (EBRT), transarterial radioembolization (TARE), and systemic-locoregional combination therapies. In the pilot exercise, expert treatment decisions showed 96.6% concordance with BEACON-HCC recommendations and 72.4% concordance with BCLC recommendations. Conclusions : BEACON-HCC is a consensus-based framework for treatment allocation that incorporates the expanding range of therapeutic options available to patients in the North American HCC population. Expert treatment decisions showed a high concordance with the BEACON-HCC system; further validation using empiric clinical data is planned through the HCC-Live Consortium.
